q: once was I a queen, But now am I a slave; in many a son I once was rich, but now am I both old And of my children reft, without a city, Forlorn, and of all mortals the most wretched.

s: Hecuba seeks vengeance against yonder guilty wretch
q: No, give me vengeance On yonder guilty wretch

s: Hecuba devises my schemes (against the murderer of my son)
q: only to my schemes Be privy, if some mischief I contrive Against the murderer of my son

s: Hecuba is mother of Cassandra (Cassandra is Agamemnon’s bedmate)
q: my daughter, who in Troy Was called Cassandra, the prophetic dame, Partakes your bed

s: Polydore is a son of Hecuba (not among those killed beneath Troy’s walls)
q: Him erst I bore and nurtured.

s: Polydore is killed by Polymestor (his guest and supposed friend)
q: The murderer was his friend, the Thracian king.

s: Agamemnon is a Greek
q: O thou light of Greece

s: Polydore is sent to Polymestor (to preserve Hecuba’s gold)
q: In this same region where his corse was found. AGA. With Polymestor, sovereign of the land? HEC. He, to preserve that execrable gold, Was hither sent

s: Polydore is denied funeral rites (his body is cast into the sea)
q: he destroyed my son, On whom he deigned not to bestow a tomb, But threw his corse into the briny deep.

s: Polyxena has received each previous solemn rite
q: To fetch you, for each previous solemn rite That best might please, if aught such rites can please, Have we performed.

s: Polymestor is a Thracian king (ruler of the region where Hecuba’s son was sent)
q: With Polymestor, sovereign of the land?

s: Polymestor is a guest_friend of Hecuba (he had been treated with respect at Ilion’s palace)
q: who ’gainst his guest Such treachery could commit, who, nor the gods Of Erebus beneath, nor those who rule In Heaven above regarding, this vile deed, Did perpetrate, e’en he with whom I oft Partook the feast, on whom I showered each bounty, Esteeming him the first of all my friends

s: Polymestor murders Polydore (after learning that Troy had fallen)
q: Yet, when at Ilion’s palace with respect He had been treated, a deliberate scheme Of murder forming, he destroyed my son

s: Polymestor possesses Priam’s treasure (his motive for receiving Hecuba’s son)
q: He, to preserve that execrable gold, Was hither sent.

s: Trojan women is a captives (seized by the Greeks)
q: These tents conceal a group of Trojan dames. AGA. Mean you those captives whom the Greeks have seized

s: Agamemnon pities Hecuba
q: To you, O Hecuba, your son, your fortunes, And your entreaties, is my pity due.

s: the Greeks captures Trojan women (as war captives)
q: those captives whom the Greeks have seized

s: the Greeks intends Greek homeward voyage (delayed by unfavorable conditions)
q: could the troops Set sail, I needs must have denied: but now, Since Neptune sends not an auspicious breeze, Expecting a more seasonable voyage, Here must we wait.

s: Ilion emits rising smoke
q: Myself a captive, am led forth to tasks Unseemly, and e’en now these eyes behold The air obscured by Ilion’s rising smoke.

s: Ilion is destroyed overthrown (after the Greek assault)
q: soon as he knew Troy was o’erthrown

s: revenge and retaliation is sought against yonder guilty wretch
q: No, give me vengeance On yonder guilty wretch

s: Justice requires punishment (for those who transgress)
q: For ’tis the common interest of mankind, Of every individual, every state, That he who hath transgressed should suffer ill.

s: Justice is a law (a divine and universal ordering principle)
q: Yet mighty are the gods, and by their law The world is ruled: for by that law we learn That there are gods, and can mark out the bounds Of justice and injustice

s: funeral rites are performed for you (previous)
q: To fetch you, for each previous solemn rite That best might please, if aught such rites can please, Have we performed.

s: Hecuba’s suffering is extreme the greatest among mortals (as Hecuba presents it)
q: Not one Exists, whose sorrows equal mine, unless You of Calamity herself would speak.

s: Agamemnon seeks to avenge Polydore (subject to avoiding blame from the Greek army)
q: I in obedience to the gods and justice Wish to avenge you on this impious friend, Could I appear your interests to espouse, Without the troops suspecting that I slay The Thracian monarch for Cassandra’s sake

s: Agamemnon is in bed with Cassandra (Cassandra is Hecuba’s daughter)
q: my daughter, who in Troy Was called Cassandra, the prophetic dame, Partakes your bed

s: Agamemnon fears the Greeks (he fears their blame and suspicion)
q: what makes me slow, Is a well-grounded fear of blame from Greece.

s: Agamemnon is ally of Polymestor (in the view of the Greek army)
q: the host esteem Him our ally

s: Agamemnon supports funeral rites (for Hecuba’s children)
q: These rites shall be performed

s: Hecuba is a former queen (now enslaved)
q: once was I a queen, But now am I a slave

s: Phrygia is no longer conspicuous in the lists of fame
q: No more, O Troy, thy dreaded name Conspicuous in the lists of fame, ’Midst fortresses impregnable shall stand,

s: Hecuba has the sepulchre of that vile brute (conspicuous to the mariner)
q: The sepulchre of that vile brute, an object Conspicuous to the mariner.

s: Polymestor has palace Polymestor’s palace
q: When from the palace I was issuing forth, This your attendant met me, and delivered The message, hearing which, I hither came.

s: Polymestor possesses Priam’s treasure (kept in his palace)
q: Is the gold He brought from Troy preserved? POLYM. I keep it safe In my own palace.

s: Polymestor possesses Polymestor’s spear
q: His massive spear suspended on the beam, No more he saw the helmets gleam.

s: Polymestor is father of sons of Polymestor
q: And the two breathless corses of his sons, Whom I, assisted by the noblest matrons Of Troy, have slain.

s: Polymestor is responsible for Polydore’s murder (for the sake of retaining his gold)
q: There was one Polydore, the youngest son Of those whom Hecuba to Priam bore; Him erst removing from the Phrygian realm, His sire to me consigned, that in my palace He might be nurtured, when that hoary king The fall of Troy suspected: him I slew

s: Polymestor loses sons of Polymestor (through Hecuba’s revenge)
q: My children’s foul and execrable murder!

s: Polymestor is enemy of Hecuba (after the murder and blinding)
q: Ah, whither am I going? wretched me! Where am I? what supports me? With these hands Groping my way like some four-footed beast, How shall I turn me, to the right or left, That I those murderous Phrygian dames may seize Who have destroyed me?

s: Phrygia has been destroyed the fall and destruction of Troy (in the Trojan War)
q: Shorn from thy rampired brow the crown Of turrets fell; thy palaces o’erspread With smoke lie waste, no more I tread Thy wonted streets, my native town.

s: Polydore is a son of Priam (youngest son)
q: There was one Polydore, the youngest son Of those whom Hecuba to Priam bore;

s: Polydore is a son of Hecuba
q: If he, my son, whom this maternal hand And his fond father in thy mansions placed, My Polydore, yet live.

s: Polydore brings the gold (from Troy)
q: Is the gold He brought from Troy preserved?

s: Priam’s treasure is kept by Polymestor (in Polymestor’s palace)
q: I keep it safe In my own palace.

s: Priam is father of Polydore (youngest son)
q: There was one Polydore, the youngest son Of those whom Hecuba to Priam bore;

s: Priam is father of Polydore
q: Him erst removing from the Phrygian realm, His sire to me consigned, that in my palace He might be nurtured, when that hoary king The fall of Troy suspected

s: Agamemnon judges Justice (in the dispute between Hecuba and Polymestor)
q: For shame attends the man who takes in hand Some great affair, and leaves it undecided. Know then, to me thou seem’st not to have slain Thy guest through an attachment to my cause, Nor yet to that of Greece, but that his gold Thou might’st retain: though in this wretched state Thou speak to serve thy interests.

s: Trojan women assist Hecuba (in taking revenge on Polymestor)
q: Whom I, assisted by the noblest matrons Of Troy, have slain.

s: Phrygia contains Minerva’s temple
q: Know’st thou where at Troy Minerva’s temple stands?

s: the Greeks are returning to Greece (after the fall of Troy)
q: for I perceive the gales Rising to waft us homeward; may success Attend the voyage to our native land!

s: Polydore’s murder motivates Justice (Hecuba’s response to Polymestor)
q: Th’ atonement he hath paid To my revenge, is just.

s: Fortune is a wavering wheel (subject to reversal)
q: for the gods Backward and forward turn her wavering wheel, And introduce confusion in the world,

s: Jove punishes Polymestor (for base deeds)
q: but by dread Jove thy foe, On him whose deeds are base, it is ordained That the severest punishments await.

s: Tyndarus’ daughter is wife of Agamemnon (queen of his royal household)
q: Her shall the wife Of Agamemnon slay, who sternly guards His royal mansion.

s: Cassandra is daughter of Hecuba
q: Cassandra too, Your daughter, must inevitably bleed.

s: Hector wields a victorious spear
q: Why, when Troy yet flourished, Why, when the city was on every side Fenced by strong bulwarks, why, when Priam lived, And Hector wielded a victorious spear,

s: Chorus urges friends
q: And in our mansions may we find all well, Freed from these dangers! CHOR. To the haven go, And to the tents, my friends, t’ endure the toils Our lords impose: for thus harsh fate enjoins.

s: Hecuba is mother of Polydore
q: If he, my son, whom this maternal hand And his fond father in thy mansions placed, My Polydore, yet live.

s: Hecuba is mother of Cassandra
q: Cassandra too, Your daughter, must inevitably bleed.

s: Hecuba is responsible for murder of Polymestor’s sons (with the assistance of Trojan women)
q: Ye shall see him Before the tent, without delay, deprived Of sight, advancing with unsteady foot, And the two breathless corses of his sons, Whom I, assisted by the noblest matrons Of Troy, have slain.

s: Hecuba has the sepulchre of that vile brute (conspicuous to the mariner)
q: The sepulchre of that vile brute, an object Conspicuous to the mariner.

s: Amphitryon is a man (mortal)
q: Is there on earth, a stranger to the man Who shared the same auspicious nuptial bed With Jove, Amphitryon born at Argos, sprung From Perseus’ son Alcæus, me the sire Of Hercules?

s: Megara is mother of children of Hercules (having borne them)
q: I these children love (And how can I help loving those I bore?) For whom I have endured the painful throes Of childbirth.

s: Hercules is a hero (renowned for extraordinary labours)
q: But what great action hath your lord performed, In having slain that hydra at the lake, Or the Nemæan lion whom with snares He caught

s: Hercules is husband of Megara (married to her in Thebes)
q: When Hercules conducted her.

s: Hercules is father of children of Hercules (deserted while completing his labours)
q: Expect ye that the father Of these deserted children, who lies stretched Amid the realms beneath will thence return

s: Hercules has house Hercules’ house (in Thebes, beside the altar)
q: SCENE.—BEFORE THE ALTAR OF JUPITER, AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE HOUSE OF HERCULES IN THEBES.

s: Hercules performs the Labours of Hercules (for Eurystheus, to rid the world of pests)
q: this great reward He on Eurystheus promised to bestow, That he would rid the world of every pest

s: Hercules undertakes Hercules’ descent to the Underworld (to retrieve Cerberus)
q: he through Tænarus’ jaws at length Went to the house of Pluto, to drag forth Into the realms of day hell’s triple hound

s: Hercules is absent in the Underworld (reported as not yet returned)
q: He thence returns not.

s: Amphitryon is sire of Hercules
q: Amphitryon born at Argos, sprung From Perseus’ son Alcæus, me the sire Of Hercules?

s: Hercules is honored by altar of Jupiter (the altar commemorates his victory over the Minyans)
q: Which my illustrious son for a memorial Of his victorious arms did here erect, When he in battle had subdued the Minyans.

s: Lycus is a tyrant (ruler of Thebes by seizure)
q: But I behold the monarch of the realm, Tyrannic Lycus

s: Lycus rules Thebes (after invading it amid civil tumult)
q: Lycus th’ egregious monarch of this land Would with the children of Alcides kill

s: Lycus seizes the throne of Thebes (after murdering Creon)
q: Lycus’ son who bears His father’s name, no Theban, but arriving From the Eubœan state, slew royal Creon, And having slain him, seized the throne

s: Lycus is murderer of Creon (killed him to take the throne)
q: From the Eubœan state, slew royal Creon, And having slain him, seized the throne

s: Lycus threatens execution of children of Hercules (to prevent future vengeance)
q: These children therefore will not I allow To live till they attain maturer years, Lest they should punish me for such a deed.
